advances: Ordinary Lebesgue volume and actual coareas at the center of an origin-symmetric body. The limiting simplex vectors need not preserve the individual cap fractions, and there is no decomposition of the body or compatibility assertion for mixed fibers.

proof:
The source is interior and symmetry gives $q_i=1/2$. By [Busemann's intersection-body theorem](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1062952/), the intersection body of $K$ is convex. Its radial value in a unit direction $u$ is $\mathcal H^{d-1}(K\cap u^\perp)$ (see [Kim–Yaskin–Zvavitch, §1 and Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1006.1546)). It is origin symmetric and full-dimensional, so its gauge $N(v)=\lVert v\rVert/\mathcal H^{d-1}(K\cap v^\perp)$ for $v\ne0$ is a norm. The identity $v_i=-\sum_{j\ne i}v_j$ gives $N(v_i)\le\sum_{j\ne i}N(v_j)$, or $p_i\le1/2$. All $p_i$ are positive.

The polytope $\lbrace p_i\in[0,1/2],\ \sum_i p_i=1\rbrace$ is the convex hull of the pair vectors $(e_j+e_k)/2$: any nonpair point has at least two fractional coordinates and lies between the two points obtained by perturbing them oppositely until a bound is reached. Iterating decreases the number of fractional coordinates. The cap formula gives $f=d2^{1/d}p$. Thus $f$ is a convex combination of the asserted pair limits, and the total weight of pairs containing $i$ is $2p_i$. The convex function $\Phi_i$ has values $d2^{-(d-1)/d}+(d-1)/2$ on such pairs and $(d-1)2^{1/(d-1)}$ on the others. Both are at most $d$ by $(1+1/r)^r\ge2$ with $r=d,d-1$ respectively, strict for $r\ge2$. The first is strict for every $d\ge2$ and its weight is positive. Jensen gives the estimate and the stated $d=2$ deficit.

For the actual realization of a pair, let its evaluation matrix initially be $(e_j-e_k)(e_j-e_k)^{\mathsf T}/2$. Mix it with weight $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ on the matrix $I/d-\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}/[d(d+1)]$. The mixture has zero row and column sums, positive diagonal entries $a_i$ of sum one, negative off-diagonals $-b_{il}$, and rank $d$ because the first matrix is positive semidefinite and the second is positive definite on $\mathbf1^\perp$. Its first $d$ rows give the coordinates of the $d+1$ vertices as columns. A dependence with coefficient sum zero annihilating those rows also annihilates the last, so it is zero by the rank condition. Row sums give centroid zero. The normals $e_1,\ldots,e_d,-\sum_{i=1}^de_i$ evaluate on these vertices as the full matrix, so the signs strictly isolate one vertex each.

Apply accepted fact be7fc2f8ef9af30d to these actual corner cuts, with total positive height one. It gives $Q_i/\sigma_i=a_i/d$ and $q_i=a_i^d/\prod_{l\ne i}(a_i+b_{il})$. Consequently the actual $f_i$ defined above is $d[\prod_{l\ne i}(a_i+b_{il})]^{1/d}$. In the pair limit the product is $1\cdot(1/2)^{d-1}$ for $j,k$ and zero elsewhere. This proves the closed convex-hull claim.
statement:
Let $d\ge2$ and $K=-K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a convex body. For $d+1$ nonzero spanning normals $v_i$ summing to zero let $q_i$ be the ordinary cap fractions through zero, $\sigma_i=\mathcal H^{d-1}(K\cap v_i^\perp)/\lVert v_i\rVert$ and $p_i=(1/\sigma_i)/\sum_j(1/\sigma_j)$. Use the actual row coordinates $f_i=d[(q_i/\sigma_i)/\sum_j(q_j/\sigma_j)]/q_i^{1/d}$ and $\Phi_i(f)=f_i+(d-1)[(\sum_{j\ne i}f_j)/d]^{d/(d-1)}$. Then $q_i=1/2$, $p_i\le1/2$, $f_i=d2^{1/d}p_i$, and
$$
\Phi_i(f)\le 2p_i[d2^{-(d-1)/d}+(d-1)/2]+(1-2p_i)(d-1)2^{1/(d-1)}<d.
$$
For $d=2$ the deficit is at least $p_i(3-2\sqrt2)>0$.

Moreover, each vector $(d2^{1/d}/2)(e_j+e_k)$ with $j\ne k$ is a limit of actual row vectors of $d$-simplices at their centroids with balanced normals strictly isolating distinct vertices. Every $f$ above belongs to the closed convex hull of such simplex vectors.
title: Strict joint-row inequalities at a symmetry center and actual simplex limits
